options.why: Read the length drawn right across the circle as a radius instead of a diameter.
Doubled the diameter instead of halving it to reach the radius.
Halved twice, dividing the diameter by $4$ rather than by $2$.
Divided by $4$, halving the length a second time.
Wrote the division the wrong way round, dividing $2$ by the diameter.
Halved a length that runs from the centre outwards and is already the radius.
Doubled the marked length, which gives the diameter rather than the radius.

questions.solution_text:
The marked line joins the centre to the circumference, so it is a radius and is not halved.
$r = 9\text{ mm}$

questions.question_text: A circular clock face has a diameter of $34$ cm. State its radius, in centimetres.

options.why: Used the stated diameter as the radius without halving it.
Doubled the diameter instead of halving it.
Divided the diameter by $4$, halving the length twice over.

questions.question_text: A lighthouse beam reaches $9$ km in every direction, sweeping out a circle of sea. State the radius of that circle, in kilometres.

options.why: Halved a distance that is measured out from the centre and is already a radius.
Doubled the distance, treating the radius as though it were a diameter.

questions.solution_text:
The beam is measured from the lighthouse at the centre, so the distance reached is a radius.
$r = 9\text{ km}$

options.why: Halved correctly but left the answer in centimetres and relabelled it as millimetres.
Converted the diameter to millimetres but forgot to halve it.
Multiplied by $100$ instead of $10$ when changing centimetres to millimetres.
Compared the two marked numbers directly without halving the diameter of circle P.
Chose the right circle but used its diameter as the radius.
Doubled the radius of circle Q, comparing a diameter with a radius.

questions.solution_text:
Circle P: $r = \frac{12}{2} = 6\text{ m}$
Circle Q: the marked line is a radius, so $r = 5\text{ m}$.
$6 > 5$, so circle P has the larger radius, $6$ m.

options.why: Took the side length of the square straight across as the radius rather than the diameter.
Doubled the side length instead of halving it to reach the radius.
Divided by $4$, halving the width of the square a second time.

questions.solution_text:
The circle touches both opposite sides, so the side length of the square is a diameter.
$d = 2.6\text{ m}$
$r = \frac{2.6}{2}$
$= 1.3\text{ m}$

questions.question_text: The diameter of a circle is $d$ centimetres. Which expression gives the radius in centimetres?

options.why: Doubled the diameter instead of dividing it by $2$.
Wrote the divisor on top, dividing $2$ by the diameter instead of the diameter by $2$.
Subtracted $2$ rather than dividing by $2$ to halve the length.

questions.solution_text:
A diameter is made of two radii, so $d = 2r$.
$r = \frac{d}{2}$
